messages: A held shot: a neon pit in a bad part of Coldwater. Two teams. A crate of foam-wrapped slag orbs. And a great deal of poor judgment.
This is Slagball. The rules are simple. You throw a slag. You hit the other side. They sit down.
If they catch it, YOU sit down, and you think about the choices that brought you here.
It was invented by bored dock hands who ran out of things to resent. It is the second-most popular sport in the basin.
The most popular sport in the basin is watching people who are worse off than you. Slagball is often both at once.
THE SUMP. A bar with a pit in the back, held together by grease, sentiment, and one very tired support beam.
Its owner, DUTCH, is a large kind man who has never won anything, including arguments with his own suppliers.
Dutch says, "Morning, Lottie. What’s the damage."
Lottie says, "The tap’s out, the drone repossessed a stool while you were asleep, and a man from a bank is standing in your pit."
Dutch says, "We don’t have a man from a bank."
Lottie says, "We do now. He brought a clipboard. Nobody brings a clipboard to say something nice."
In the pit stands VESS — sharp, pressed, holding a clipboard like a weapon she is licensed to carry.
Vess says, "Are you Dutch? The Dutch who owns this — establishment?"
Dutch says, "Depends who’s asking and how much they’re asking for."
Vess says, "I’m asking for forty thousand credits, and I’m asking today, and my name is Vess."
Dutch says, "Well, Vess, I’ve got about forty credits and a lot of what I’d call ambiance."
Vess says, "The bank calls it a fire hazard with a liquor license."
Lottie says, "She’s not wrong, Dutch."
Dutch says, "Lottie, whose side are you on."
Lottie says, "The side that still has a roof. I’m flexible about which side that is."
Vess produces a stylus and begins itemizing the Sump the way a coroner itemizes a body.
Vess says, "One bar, structurally optimistic. One pit, purpose unclear. Fourteen stools, one recently repossessed. And a smell I’m choosing not to catalogue for legal reasons."
Dutch says, "That smell is character."
Vess says, "Character doesn’t pay a lien, Dutch. I’ve tried. I once billed a man’s personality. It bounced."
Dutch says, "You bill personalities?"
Vess says, "I bill everything. It’s the only language the bank speaks and I’m fluent and I hate it."
A regular at the end of the bar quietly finishes his drink, sets down exactly no credits, and leaves. Dutch watches him go with the fondness of a man being robbed by family.
Dutch says, "That’s Old Pemms. He hasn’t paid since the Waking. He’s basically furniture."
Lottie says, "Furniture we can’t repossess because he’s technically alive. We checked. Twice. Hopefully."
Vess says, "This is the worst-run business I have ever been sent to close, and I closed a clinic that was legally a boat."
Dutch says, "And yet you’re still standing in my pit."
Vess says, "The exit’s behind Old Pemms and I’m not ready to have that conversation."
APEX. A fitness-arena empire so glossy you can see your own inadequacy in the floor. At its summit: MAXIM VIGO.
VIGO is speaking. VIGO is always speaking. Currently he is speaking to a hologram of himself, which is the only audience that has never let him down.
Maxim Vigo says, "Look at us. Look at what we’ve optimized. There is not one soft thing left in this entire tower. Not one."
Maxim Vigo says, "Softness is just strength that gave up early. I read that. I think I said it. I’ll have someone check who said it and then I’ll have said it."
An assistant approaches, terrified in the specific way of people paid well to be terrified.
Maxim Vigo says, "Tell me something optimized."
Vess says, "Sir, the Sump acquisition. The owner can’t pay. Foreclosure clears in thirty days. The whole block is ours."
Maxim Vigo says, "The Sump. That grease-stain with a pit. I want it flattened and turned into an APEX Wellness Annex."
Maxim Vigo says, "Do you know what people need, Vess? People need to be told they are almost good enough, forever, for a monthly fee."
Vess says, "That’s — genuinely the darkest thing I’ve heard in a boardroom, and I do foreclosures."
Maxim Vigo says, "Thank you. Put it on a banner."
VIGO admires his own jaw in the window, which is a thing his jaw is very used to.
Maxim Vigo says, "Nobody has ever beaten me at anything. Do you know why? Because I only enter things I have already bought."
Maxim Vigo says, "That’s not cheating. That’s pre-winning. Legal team loves it. Put THAT on a banner too. I’m on fire today."
The hologram of Vigo nods along, because it is programmed to, and because it, too, has never been told no.
Maxim Vigo says, "You agree. Of course you agree. You’re the only one in this building with taste, and you’re me."
Vess says, "Sir, should I be worried you only take counsel from a projection of yourself?"
Maxim Vigo says, "Worried? Vess, it’s the most efficient relationship I’ve ever had. He never asks for a raise and he agrees with me at the speed of light. Literally. He’s light."
Vess says, "That’s — I’m going to write "concerning" in my notes and move on."
Maxim Vigo says, "Write "visionary." Cross out "concerning." Actually, fire whoever taught you the word "concerning." It’s soft. It’s a soft word."
Vigo strides to a wall of screens showing every APEX arena in the basin, all identical, all optimized, all empty of anything a person would call joy.
Maxim Vigo says, "Look at it. A hundred arenas. Not one of them has a pit. Do you know why? Because a pit is where the poor go to feel like they matter, and mattering is not a subscription tier."
Vess says, "You could add a mattering tier."
Maxim Vigo says, "Don’t tempt me with a good idea before lunch, Vess. Flatten the Sump. I want the whole basin optimized before I have to feel anything about any of it."
Vess returns to the Sump to deliver the papers. She does not expect to feel anything. This is, professionally, the plan.
Vess says, "Thirty days, Dutch. Raise forty thousand or the block goes to APEX and this pit becomes a place where people feel bad about their cores."
Dutch says, "Forty thousand. I could sell everything I own and get to about nine."
Vess says, "Then I’d stop at nine. Save yourself the everything."
A regular — GILES — looks up from the bar, heartbroken already, which is his natural resting state.
Giles says, "They can’t take the Sump. I met the love of my life here."
Lottie says, "Giles, you met the love of your life here eleven times. Three of them left through that window."
Giles says, "And I’d wait for all of them to come back. That’s what the Sump IS, Lottie. It’s a place you come back to."
It is, briefly, moving. Then a support beam groans, and everyone flinches on instinct.
Dutch says, "Vess. Off the record. Is there any way — any way at all — a place like this beats a thing like APEX?"
Vess says, "Off the record? No. On the record, also no, but with a stamp."
Vess says, "You’d need a miracle, a lawyer, and forty thousand credits, and you have a beam that’s actively quitting."
Dutch says, "What if I told you I could get you the lawyer for free."
Vess says, "I’d say you don’t have that kind of charm."
Dutch says, "No. But the Sump does. Everybody who works here started as a customer who couldn’t afford to leave."
Vess looks at the papers. Vess looks at the pit. Something professional in her sets down its clipboard, just for a second.
Vess says, "Get me a reason. A real one. And I’ll pretend I forgot which side I’m on for exactly as long as it’s interesting."
Giles says, "I have a reason. Her name was Marisol. Or Deb. It was one of the two and they both left through the window."
Lottie says, "Giles, nobody is asking about the window women right now."
Giles says, "Somebody should. Somebody always should. That’s the tragedy of the Sump, Lottie: too many windows, not enough staying."
Vess says, "Is he always like this?"
Dutch says, "Only when he’s awake. Asleep he’s worse. He narrates."
Old Pemms, still furniture, raises a finger as though to contribute, thinks better of it, and lowers it. It is the most anyone has ever heard from Old Pemms.
Dutch says, "See that? Even Pemms cares. Pemms hasn’t cared about anything since they took the sun private."
Vess says, "That is the lowest bar for hope I have ever been asked to clear, and yet."
Dutch says, "That’s the Sump’s whole business model, Vess. The lowest bar, cleared by people who had no business jumping."
That night, PIP — the anxious kid who buses the tables — is watching a flyer flicker on the wall.
Pip says, "Dutch? Dutch, um. This is probably nothing. It’s definitely nothing. I’ll go."
Dutch says, "Pip. Breathe. What is it."
Pip says, "The Coldwater Slagball Open. Grand prize is — it’s forty thousand credits. It’s exactly forty thousand credits."
The whole bar turns and looks at the flyer as if it had personally arrived to save them, which, narratively, it has.
Lottie says, "That’s not a coincidence. That’s a screenwriter."
Dutch says, "We enter a Slagball tournament. We win exactly what we owe. We keep the Sump."
Vess says, "Do any of you play Slagball?"
A long silence. Somewhere, the tired support beam creaks, as if to answer for them.
Dutch says, "We own a Slagball pit."
Vess says, "Owning a pit is not playing Slagball. I own a treadmill. I am not a horse."
Giles says, "I’ve always wanted to be part of a team. A team is just a group of people who agree to be disappointed together."
Lottie says, "Giles, that’s a family. A team’s the one where you win sometimes."
Dutch says, "Then we win sometimes. Starting now. Who’s in."
Hands go up. Slowly. Reluctantly. The way hands go up when they know the rest of the body disagrees.
Pip says, "I’ll — I’ll do the thing. The team thing. Please don’t make me talk to the crowd."
Dutch says, "Pip, you’re in. Merv?"
MERV, an enormous man who has said nine words this year, considers the question with great seriousness.
Merv says, "Fine."
Dutch says, "That’s five words. He’s excited."
Lottie says, "I’m in. I’ve been throwing things at men in this bar for twenty years without a trophy to show for it. Time it counted."
Dutch says, "Lottie, you throw glasses."
Lottie says, "And I’ve never missed. You do the math on who your best player is and then apologize to me for the wage."
Giles says, "I’m in too. If the Sump goes down, I want to have loved it out loud at least once, in a uniform, on a team."
Dutch says, "Giles, you understand people will be throwing things at you."
Giles says, "Dutch. People have been throwing things at me my whole life. At least in the pit it’ll finally be regulation."
Vess says, "That is either the saddest or the healthiest thing I’ve heard all week and I genuinely cannot tell which."
Dutch says, "At the Sump those are the same thing. You’ll get used to it. Or you’ll leave through the window, and we’ll name a stool after you."
Pip says, "Do we — do we get uniforms? I don’t want a number that draws attention. Can I be a low number? A shy number?"
Dutch says, "Pip, you can be whatever number won’t make you faint. We’ll workshop it."
A team needs six. The Sump has five and a half, if you count Giles as a whole person, which the Sump generously does.
The sixth arrives on his own. He always does. His name — he insists — is BARNACLE BASH.
Barnacle Bash says, "Ahoy the pit! I heard there be a crew forming, and a crew be needing a man who fears no water!"
Lottie says, "Bash. There’s no water. There’s never been water. It’s a bar."
Barnacle Bash says, "That be exactly what the sea WANTS ye to think, Lottie."
Dutch says, "Bash, are you actually a pirate?"
Barnacle Bash says, "I be as much a pirate as this be a ship, captain. Which is to say: completely, and only me."
Pip says, "I think he’s the most confident person I’ve ever met and I find it deeply calming."
Barnacle Bash says, "The boy has SEA SENSE! Ye there, cabin boy — stick by ol’ Bash and ye’ll never drown on dry land, which be the most common way to drown in this city!"
Pip says, "That’s — genuinely reassuring? I don’t know why. I feel safer. Is that wrong?"
Lottie says, "It’s wrong, but it’s the good kind of wrong. Bash has never once been right and never once been scared. There’s a lesson in there if you don’t look at it directly."
Barnacle Bash says, "Aye! Fear be a fog, and a good captain simply declines to sail through it! I declined years ago! Look at me now — landlocked, beloved, and TERRIFYING at slagball!"
Dutch says, "He’s not wrong about the terrifying part. I’ve seen him throw. Grown collectors have crossed the street."
Dutch says, "He throws harder than anyone in the block. I stopped asking questions the day he called the ice machine a kraken and won."
Vess reviews the roster with the expression of a woman watching a bridge get built out of chairs.
Vess says, "A frightened boy. A silent mountain. A waitress with a grudge. A romantic with a concussion history. A pirate. And you."
Dutch says, "And you."
Vess says, "I’m the LAWYER. I hold the clipboard. I do not enter the pit."
Dutch says, "The rules say six players on the roster, minimum, or you’re disqualified. We have six. If one of us so much as sneezes, we forfeit."
Vess says, "So I’m the sneeze insurance."
Dutch says, "You’re the seventh. The one who catches us when we fall. Legally. And, I’m hoping, a little bit in general."
Vess says, "Don’t. I have a clipboard and I’m not afraid to file it."
But she signs the roster. In the box marked RESERVE she writes her name, and underlines it, and pretends the underline was an accident.
Barnacle Bash says, "A fine crew! But a crew needs a NAME, captain. Every vessel that ever sailed had a name to curse when she sank!"
Dutch says, "We’re the Sump."
Barnacle Bash says, "That be a berth, not a name! We need somethin’ to strike fear! The Drowned Fists! The Kraken’s Regret!"
Lottie says, "The Kraken’s Regret is what I call the men’s room after darts night."
Pip says, "What about — and this is dumb — what about "The Sump"? Because that’s what we are and nobody expects the thing that’s just true."
A silence. It is, everyone realizes, perfect. The most dangerous thing a Coldwater team can be is exactly what it says on the door.
Dutch says, "The Sump it is. Pip named the team. Pip, you’ve done one confident thing and I’m very proud."
Pip says, "I’m already regretting it. Can we go back to the fear one?"
Merv says, "No."
Dutch says, "Merv likes it. That settles it. When Merv talks, the ceiling listens."
You cannot win the Open without a coach. Every good coach in Coldwater is expensive. So the Sump finds a bad one who used to be great.
COACH RUSK. Once the finest slagger in the basin. Now a wreck on a busted hover-chair that lists permanently to port.
Coach Rusk says, "Get out. I don’t coach. I retired. I sit here and I resent the ceiling. It’s a full schedule."
Dutch says, "They say you never lost a match."
Coach Rusk says, "They say a lot of things. They also say this chair is fixable, and look at me listing into the fern."
Dutch says, "We need a coach. We’ve got thirty days, no skill, and a beam that’s given up."
Coach Rusk says, "Then you don’t need a coach. You need a priest and a good lawyer."
Vess says, "She’s here. She’s expensive. Coach us and she stays free, which is the only free thing in this economy."
Rusk looks at the six of them. His eyes, ancient and mean, do a thing they have not done in years: they light up, out of pure contempt.
Coach Rusk says, "You’re all terrible. I can see it from here. The big one’s got no killer instinct, the kid flinches at his own shadow, and the pirate’s a lawsuit."
Barnacle Bash says, "A COMPLIMENT!"
Coach Rusk says, "It was not."
Coach Rusk says, "But terrible I can work with. Terrible’s just great that hasn’t been screamed at yet. Champions I can’t fix. You? You’re all wet clay and low standards. Perfect."
Dutch says, "Is that a yes?"
Coach Rusk says, "It’s a maybe with the volume of a yes. Wheel me to the pit. And somebody get me out of this fern, I’ve been in it since the spring."
They extract Coach Rusk from the fern. Bits of fern come with him. He does not remove them for the rest of the picture. It becomes, in time, a look.
Pip says, "Sir, is it true you once won a match with a broken arm?"
Coach Rusk says, "Both arms, boy. And a grudge. The grudge did most of it. Never underestimate a well-kept grudge; it’s the only thing in Coldwater that appreciates in value."
Giles says, "Coach, what happened? You were the greatest. What takes a legend down to a fern?"

Coach Rusk says, "Same thing that takes everybody down, romantic. I won everything, and then I had nothing left to be angry at, and a man who runs on anger can’t coast. So I sat down. In a fern, as it turns out."
Dutch says, "So what changed today?"
Coach Rusk says, "You walked in with six of the worst players I’ve ever seen and asked me to save a bar. That’s the first thing worth being angry about in nine years. Thank you. I hate it. Let’s go."
Barnacle Bash says, "A captain who runs on fury! I’ll follow ye into any storm, ye landlocked terror!"
Coach Rusk says, "The pirate’s going to be a problem and I’ve decided he’s my favorite. Wheel. Pit. Now."
Rusk’s methods are unorthodox. By which the survivors mean cruel. By which Rusk means effective.
Coach Rusk says, "Rule one. In the pit, everything is trying to hit you. The slag. The crowd. Your own doubt. Your own mother, if she’s in the stands, and mine always was."
Coach Rusk says, "So you learn to not be where the throw is going. That’s the whole game. Not being there. I built a career on not being there. Ask my kids."
He gestures. A battered repossession drone — UNIT 7, the one that took the stool — hovers in, reprogrammed and furious.
Coach Rusk says, "This is Unit 7. It used to take furniture. Now it takes SLAGS, and it throws them at your soft little heads. Dodge, or learn."
Pip says, "That’s a repossession drone. That is a WEAPON."
Coach Rusk says, "If you can dodge a repo-drone, boy, you can dodge a slag. And if you can’t dodge a repo-drone — you were going to lose your couch anyway."
Unit 7 opens fire. Pip is struck immediately, in the face, with great enthusiasm.
Pip says, "I felt that in my ancestors."
Coach Rusk says, "Good. Pain’s just the drone teaching. Free lessons. In this economy you take the free ones. Again."
MERV steps up. Unit 7 fires. Merv does not dodge. Merv catches the slag one-handed and crushes it, and the drone, out of respect, backs up.
Coach Rusk says, "Now HIM I don’t have to teach. Him I have to aim."
Merv says, "Okay."
LOTTIE takes the pit. She has spent twenty years dodging drunks, pinches, and thrown glasses. The drone stands no chance and seems to know it.
Lottie says, "Sweetheart, I’ve dodged worse than you on a slow Tuesday."
Coach Rusk says, "The waitress is our best player and she started this morning. That’s not a good sign about the rest of you. That’s a GREAT sign about her."
GILES, meanwhile, is hit by a slag Unit 7 did not throw. It is unclear where it came from. It happens to Giles a lot.
Giles says, "Coach, I think the universe is a slag and I am the pit."
Coach Rusk says, "Finally. The romantic gets it. That’s the only true thing anyone’s said in this dump all week."
Rusk introduces the second drill. He calls it "Trust." It involves standing very still while Merv throws a slag as hard as he can at a plank six inches from your head.
Coach Rusk says, "The plank is the lesson, Pip. You flinch, you lose. You trust the drill, you learn where you end and the throw begins. That line’s the whole sport."
Pip says, "The plank has a hole in it shaped exactly like a slag."
Coach Rusk says, "That’s Merv’s work. He’s never missed the plank. He’s also never hit the plank on purpose. He simply asks it to move and it declines. Watch."
Merv throws. The slag goes through the existing hole in the plank without touching the sides, and Pip does not flinch, because Pip has fainted, which Rusk marks down as progress.
Coach Rusk says, "Fainting’s just flinching that committed. We can work with commitment. Wake him up and do it again."
Barnacle Bash says, "COACH! Teach me to throw so hard the SEA apologizes!"
Coach Rusk says, "Bash, you already throw too hard. Your problem isn’t power, it’s that you announce every throw with a nautical war crime. The other team hears you coming from the docks."
Barnacle Bash says, "The announcin’ is HALF the throw, coach!"
Coach Rusk says, "It’s a third of the throw and all of the lawsuit. Fine. Keep the shanty. We’ll weaponize the confusion. Nobody’s ever game-planned for a man who thinks the ice machine is a kraken."
Days pass. Bruises bloom and fade. The six of them are, against all decency, getting less terrible.
Coach Rusk says, "You’re still bad. But you’re bad on PURPOSE now. That’s technique. Bad on purpose is a plan. Bad by accident is just Tuesday."
Dutch says, "Coach. Do you think we can actually win this thing?"
Coach Rusk says, "No."
Dutch says, "Oh."
Coach Rusk says, "But I didn’t think I’d get out of that fern either, and here I am, listing at you with hope. Wheel me closer, I’m being sincere and I hate it."
One last drill, the night before the Open. Rusk lines all six of them along the pit and turns off the neon, so they train the way champions die: in the dark.
Coach Rusk says, "The eyes lie. In a real match the crowd, the lights, the money on the board — all of it’s screaming at your eyes. So we learn to play without them tonight."
Pip says, "How do we throw at something we can’t see?"
Coach Rusk says, "You listen for the thing that’s sure it can’t lose. Certainty’s loud, kid. Rich certainty is the loudest thing in any room. You aim at the smug and you rarely miss."
In the dark, Merv catches a slag he could not possibly have seen, out of pure enormous instinct, and hands it back into the black like a gift.
Merv says, "Easy."
Coach Rusk says, "The mountain speaks and the lesson’s over. Everybody drink water. Not you, Bash, you’ll say something."
Barnacle Bash says, "The sea is water and I AM the sea, coach!"
Coach Rusk says, "And there it is. Bed. All of you. Tomorrow we find out if terrible-on-purpose is a plan or an obituary."
Before they go, Rusk keeps Dutch back a moment in the dark pit.

Coach Rusk says, "You know why I never lost, Dutch? Not talent. There were more talented sluggers than me. I never lost because I never once thought I deserved to win. Kept me hungry. Kept me watching."
Dutch says, "That sounds miserable, Coach."

Coach Rusk says, "It was. But your lot’s got the same disease and they don’t even know it. Not one of them thinks they deserve a thing. That’s why they might just take everything. The world never sees the undeserving coming."
Dutch says, "And you? You think you deserve tomorrow?"
Coach Rusk says, "I think I deserve to yell one more time in a full arena before this chair finally lists all the way into the ground. That’s enough. That’s more than the fern was going to give me."
The Open. A neon arena. And, in a broadcast booth built for two and a budget for less, the voice of Sub-Channel 2½.
Blurt says, "Welcome, welcome, to the Coldwater Slagball Open, live on Sub-Channel Two and a Half, the ONLY channel that could afford us!"
Cass says, "Blurt, I want to say, before the violence starts, that my contract is up for renewal and I have made peace with dying in this booth."
Blurt says, "That’s the spirit, Cass! First up — the plucky no-names from the Sump versus a team of sentient gym equipment!"
Round one. The Sump versus APEX’s warm-up squad: six identical men who have never once been told no.
The Ref says, "Both teams to the line. Slags in the middle. On my whistle. And please — please — nobody dies. I have to write the report."
The whistle. Chaos. Bash bellows a sea-shanty and hurls a slag hard enough to change a man’s religion.
Barnacle Bash says, "DOWN YE GO, LANDLUBBER, AND GIVE ME REGARDS TO THE DEEP!"
Cass says, "He knocked one out cold and there’s no water anywhere near here. I’ve stopped asking. It’s healthier."
Pip, terrified, closes his eyes and throws blind. It hits the last APEX clone square between his optimized eyes.
Pip says, "Did I — did I do it? I can’t look. Is it good or is it the worst thing I’ve ever done?"
Coach Rusk says, "It’s good, kid. For once the two are the same thing. Open your eyes. We won a round."
Blurt says, "UPSET! The Sump takes round one! Somewhere an accountant is confused and a pirate is very, very happy!"
Cass says, "Blurt, I have covered eleven sports on this channel and nine of them were illegal. I have never seen a team win by simply refusing to understand they should lose."
Blurt says, "It’s the Coldwater way, Cass! You don’t beat the odds, you just annoy them until they leave!"
Round two. The Sump draws a team of retired debt collectors — men who throw for a living and enjoy it too much.
Lottie says, "Oh, I know these boys. They repossessed my mother’s teeth. This one’s personal and I’m going to enjoy it."
Lottie clears three of them before they set their feet. It is less a sporting performance than a settling of accounts.
Blurt says, "THE WAITRESS IS UNTOUCHABLE! She’s throwing like the rent’s due, Cass, and for her it always is!"
Cass says, "I’m told she’s never received a tip commensurate with that arm and honestly that’s the real crime on display tonight."
Round three. Giles is eliminated in four seconds by a slag that ricochets off the ceiling, a wall, and his own teammate before finding him. Even the ref looks impressed.
Giles says, "It found me. It always finds me. I’ve made my peace. Tell Marisol. Or Deb. Tell the window."
The Ref says, "Kid, in twenty years of officiating I have never seen the game itself hold a grudge against one player. You should see someone. Or an astronomer."
The semifinal. The Sump versus a corporate development squad in matching APEX warmups, all named some variety of "Chad" for optimization purposes.
Blurt says, "And here come the APEX juniors, Cass — six young men bred in a lab to have excellent cores and no interior lives whatsoever!"
Cass says, "They move as one, Blurt. It’s beautiful and it’s deeply upsetting, like a school of fish that files taxes."
Merv steps to the line alone against all six. He does not throw. He simply catches everything they send, and sends it back, and the juniors sit down in perfect synchronized disappointment.
Blurt says, "THE MOUNTAIN CATCHES EVERYTHING! Six optimized Chads, one silent man, and the man is winning, Cass!"
Merv says, "Sit."
Cass says, "He said "sit" and they SAT. That’s not a throw, that’s a command. I’ve never respected anyone more and I’ve interviewed a warlord."
Coach Rusk says, "THAT’S my mountain! Aim him at the final, Dutch, that’s all I ever have to do — point Merv at the problem and get out of the splash zone!"
The Sump takes the semifinal. In the tunnel, the six of them stand together, filthy and bruised and one win from the impossible, and none of them say anything for a long moment.
Dutch says, "One more. One more match and the Sump is ours forever."
Pip says, "I haven’t fainted in two whole rounds, Dutch. That’s a personal record. I’m calling my mom. She won’t believe it. I don’t believe it."
Giles says, "I got hit forty times today and I have never felt more alive. Is that the game, Dutch? Is that what everyone’s been getting?"
Lottie says, "That’s it, Giles. That’s the whole thing. You get hit, you get up, you find out you’re still here. Some people pay a gym for that. We just open the doors."
Merv says, "Together."
Everyone turns. Merv has said a fourth word this year, and it is the right one, and nobody makes a joke, because some words you just let stand.
Round after round, the Sump crawls up the bracket. They are not good. They are stubborn, which in Coldwater beats good more often than good would like.
High in a private box, MAXIM VIGO watches the scrappy little bar refuse to be flattened on schedule, and his optimized jaw begins, very slightly, to clench.
Maxim Vigo says, "Who ARE these people. Why won’t they lose. Losing is the natural state of the poor, it’s practically a service we provide."
Vess says, "They’re winning, sir. It happens. Occasionally. To people who aren’t you."
Maxim Vigo says, "Then buy their coach. Buy their bar. Buy their WATER — the pirate seems to need it."
Vess says, "There is no water, sir."
Maxim Vigo says, "Then buy that too. I want a monopoly on things that don’t exist. That’s called futures, Vess. That’s called vision."
Vigo descends to the arena floor to intimidate the Sump in person, which is a thing winners are never supposed to need to do.
Maxim Vigo says, "Enjoy the little rounds. My real team hasn’t played yet. APEX PRIME doesn’t enter until the final. We conserve. We optimize. We arrive."
Dutch says, "Six warm-up squads and you haven’t won a single round against us yet."
Maxim Vigo says, "Those weren’t my A-squad. Or my B-squad. Frankly they weren’t squads, they were a tax write-off with legs."
Coach Rusk says, "I know you. Vigo. You bought the league I used to play in and turned it into a gym with ads. You’re the reason a sport became a subscription."
Maxim Vigo says, "Rusk. They told me you died in a fern."
Coach Rusk says, "I got better. Out of spite. It’s the only exercise you can’t sell, Vigo, and it’s the only one that ever mattered."
Maxim Vigo says, "Charming. Old anger in an old chair. When my Prime team flattens your bar of misfits, I’ll have you both mounted in the lobby. Tastefully. With a QR code."
Coach Rusk says, "Wheel me at him, Dutch. Wheel me at him RIGHT now."
Dutch says, "Coach, no. That’s exactly the round he’d win."
The night before the final, Unit 7 malfunctions in the pit during practice — reprogrammed AGAIN, this time by a very expensive hand.
It fires a live rivet instead of a slag. Rusk shoves Dutch clear, takes the hit himself, and his listing chair finally lists all the way over.
Dutch says, "Coach! Coach — somebody get a medic — Rusk, stay with me —"
Coach Rusk says, "Relax. I’ve been hit by worse. I once got benched by a slag to the throat in the ’61 final and married the medic. Bad news is I can’t coach you tomorrow."
Dutch says, "Then we don’t play. I’m not doing it without you."
Coach Rusk says, "You ABSOLUTELY are, you enormous coward. You think I dragged myself out of that fern so you could quit the day before?"
Vess storms in, clipboard shaking, holding a maintenance log with one very expensive fingerprint on it.
Vess says, "It was APEX. Vigo reprogrammed the drone. I have the log. I have the fingerprint. I have — I have a CONSCIENCE now, apparently, which was not in my contract."
Dutch says, "You could lose your job for bringing me this."
Vess says, "I already quit. Loudly. In the elevator, to a hologram of him, which was oddly satisfying and slightly his fault."
Rusk, flat on his back and grinning like a wolf, waves them all in close.
Coach Rusk says, "Listen. All of you. I can’t be in the pit tomorrow. So one of you has to be me. Mean. Certain. Impossible to hit and worse to face."
Coach Rusk says, "It’s not about the slag. It was never about the slag. It’s about being the last one standing in a place that told you to sit down your whole life."

Coach Rusk says, "Now the Sump plays tomorrow. With or without me, with or without the beam, with or without a single reason to believe it. Especially without the reason. That’s the good kind of winning."
Dutch says, "Okay. Okay. We play. Vess — you’re on the roster now. We just lost our sneeze insurance."
Vess says, "I don’t play Slagball."
Dutch says, "None of us do. That’s never once stopped us. Welcome to the Sump."
That night nobody sleeps. Rusk holds court from a cot in the back of the bar, wired with painkillers and opinions.
Coach Rusk says, "Listen. Vigo thinks he broke us tonight. Good. Let him. A man who thinks he’s already won stops watching his own feet."
Pip says, "But we ARE broken, coach. Our coach is on a cot. Our lawyer’s our sixth player. I fainted during the semifinal and I was a spectator."
Coach Rusk says, "Pip. Come here. What’s the one thing every single person in this bar has in common?"
Pip says, "We’re all going to lose our home?"
Coach Rusk says, "Before that."
Giles says, "We were all left through a window?"
Coach Rusk says, "Before THAT. You’re all people this city already counted out. Nobody’s expecting anything from you. That’s not a weakness, you soft sad wonderful idiots. That’s CAMOUFLAGE."
Lottie says, "He’s got a point. Nobody watches the busboy. Nobody guards the waitress. Nobody game-plans the man who thinks the ice machine is a kraken."
Barnacle Bash says, "It IS a kraken, Lottie, and tomorrow it fights beside us in spirit."
Dutch says, "Get some rest. All of you. Tomorrow the whole city finds out what happens when the people it forgot about show up to collect."
The championship. On one side: APEX PRIME, six professionals so enhanced they no longer technically require sleep or empathy.
On the other: a bankrupt bar, a fainting boy, a pirate, a silent giant, a waitress, a heartbroken man, and a lawyer who forgot which side she was on and never went back.
Blurt says, "This is IT, Cass! The final! The corporate juggernaut versus the little pit that wouldn’t quit! I have goosebumps and one of them is on my eye!"
Cass says, "Blurt, if we survive this broadcast, I want you to know you were the only good thing about Sub-Channel Two and a Half."
Blurt says, "Cass, that’s beautiful. We are contractually eleven minutes from the ad break. Hold that thought and your bladder."
MAXIM VIGO struts to center pit in a custom uniform that cost more than the Sump’s entire debt, which is a fact he has printed on the back of it.
Maxim Vigo says, "Dutch. Before we begin. I want you to know there is no version of this where you win. I bought the arena. I bought the slags. I may have bought the ref."
The Ref says, "You did not buy the ref. The ref makes forty credits a night and hates every one of you equally. It’s the only fair thing left in this city."
Maxim Vigo says, "A holdout. Charming. Flatten him after."
Dutch says, "Vigo. You can buy the arena and the slags and the beam over our heads. You know the one thing about the Sump you could never afford?"
Maxim Vigo says, "Please. I’m optimized. I can afford a feeling if I want one. I’ll have someone feel it for me."
Dutch says, "You could never afford to NEED it. Everyone in this pit needs each other. That’s not for sale. That’s just the bill nobody sends you."
It is a good line. Even Vess writes it down. Even Vigo, for one flickering second, looks like a man who owns everything and none of it.
Maxim Vigo says, "That’s — very moving. Truly. I felt a thing. I’ll have it removed later. But I felt it."
Dutch says, "That’s all I wanted, Vigo. One real thing before we beat you."
Maxim Vigo says, "You won’t beat me. You’ll lose beautifully and I’ll clip it for the annex opening. "Even the plucky lose." It tests well with subscribers."
Coach Rusk says, "Keep talking, Vigo. My whole team plays better when someone rich is certain. It’s the loudest sound in the pit and my mountain throws at loud."
Maxim Vigo says, "Whistle."
The whistle. APEX PRIME is everything the Sump is not: fast, precise, merciless, moisturized.
One by one the Sump goes down. Bash, hurling shanties, is caught mid-boast. Giles is hit by a slag from his own side, somehow, again.
Giles says, "Even now. Even in the final. The universe is a slag. I have made peace with being the pit."
Cass says, "The romantic is out and honestly he looks relieved. It’s the calmest anyone has been in this arena all night."
Pip faints from nerves. Merv is triple-teamed and buried under slags, going down like a demolished tower, slowly and with dignity.
Blurt says, "It’s falling apart, Cass! It’s five to two! Then five to — oh no — it’s APEX PRIME, all six, versus the Sump’s last two!"
Two left for the Sump: DUTCH, who has never won anything, and VESS, who has never played anything, standing back to back in a pit at the end of the world.
Vess says, "Dutch. I want you to know, as your lawyer, that this is a catastrophically bad position."
Dutch says, "I know."
Vess says, "And as your — as whatever the other thing is — I’ve never been happier to be in a catastrophically bad position with anyone."
Dutch says, "Vess. Was that a feeling?"
Vess says, "File it. We’ll deal with it if we live. Incoming."
APEX PRIME advances in formation, a wall of optimized men who have practiced this exact humiliation in a lab.
Maxim Vigo says, "End it. Slowly. I want the broadcast to have time for my sponsors."
From his cot at the rail, hooked to a monitor and running purely on grievance, Coach Rusk finds his voice for the last drill he has left.
Coach Rusk says, "DUTCH! Two of you left! That’s not a loss, that’s a CORNER! Everybody wins from a corner or they were never going to win at all!"
Dutch says, "Coach, there are six of them and two of us!"

Coach Rusk says, "Then the math is finally simple enough for you to understand! Every throw you make has to count and every throw they make they’ll take for granted! Make them spend! Make them SPEND, Dutch!"
Dutch catches a lazy, arrogant throw one-handed — a throw APEX PRIME made because they assumed the round was over — and the thrower sits down, stunned, optimized right out of the game.
Blurt says, "CAUGHT! Dutch catches one and it’s five on two — no — it’s FIVE ON TWO but the Sump has the momentum and the crowd and possibly a god!"
Cass says, "The rich team just learned that "taking it for granted" is a move you can lose to. I’m going to cry again. Renew my contract."
Five on two becomes four on two becomes three on two. The Sump spends every throw like it’s the last credit in the till, because it is.
Bash, seated on the sideline and eliminated, coaches the only way he knows how.
Barnacle Bash says, "STEADY, CAPTAIN! The bigger the ship, the slower she turns! Make ‘em turn! Make the whole fat galleon come about!"
Dutch says, "That’s — actually good advice, Bash?"
Barnacle Bash says, "I have been giving good advice for YEARS, captain, ye simply keep bein’ on land when I say it!"
Vess, who has never thrown a slag in her life, catches one purely by refusing to move — an accident of stubbornness that eliminates an APEX Prime striker.
Vess says, "I didn’t mean to do that. I froze. I froze and it worked. Is that a technique? Is "legally paralyzed" a technique?"
Coach Rusk says, "In this sport, counselor? It’s a Hall of Fame technique. The plank never moves either. Be the plank. BE THE PLANK, VESS."
Vess says, "I went to law school to avoid being the plank and here I am, being the plank, and loving it. My mother was right about everything."
The score locks. By ancient Slagball law, a deadlock at the final invokes SUDDEN DARK: the arena lights cut, and the last players throw by sound alone.
The Ref says, "Sudden Dark! House lights down! One throw each! Last team standing takes the Open! And may whatever’s left of your gods have mercy!"
Blackout. The arena is a held breath. Somewhere in the dark, six optimized professionals and two amateurs, and only the sound of a city that has always thrown things at people like the Sump.

Coach Rusk says, "Dutch! DUTCH! Don’t aim with your eyes, you never had the eyes! Aim with the part of you that’s been ducking this city your whole life! LISTEN for the ones who think they can’t lose — they breathe loud!"
And in the dark, Dutch — who has lost at everything, who has ducked every collector, every landlord, every disappointment — closes his eyes he doesn’t need anyway, and listens.
He hears six professionals breathing the smug, even breath of men who have never once needed anything. And he throws at the smuggest breath in the room.
Maxim Vigo says, "This is absurd. Lights! Somebody turn the LIGHTS on! I paid for those lights! I own the photons!"
The Ref says, "Sudden Dark is in the charter you signed, Mr. Vigo. Page forty. Nobody reads page forty. I read page forty. It’s the only power I have and tonight it is enormous."
Maxim Vigo says, "My men can’t optimize what they can’t SEE!"

Coach Rusk says, "No, Vigo. They can’t. That’s the whole point of the dark. It takes away every advantage a man can buy and leaves only the ones he had to earn. You never taught them to earn. You bought them finished."
In the black, an APEX striker throws at a sound and hits his own captain. A second throws at that sound and hits the first. Certainty, in the dark, eats itself.
Blurt says, "Cass, I genuinely cannot see the pit, I am describing this game entirely by the noises, and the noises are GLORIOUS."
Cass says, "It sounds like a filing cabinet falling down a stairwell forever, Blurt, and it is the finest thing I have ever called."
A sound. Contact. A body sitting down hard in the dark. Then another. Then — impossibly — a chain of them, as APEX PRIME, unable to see, panics and catches its own friendly fire.
Blurt says, "I CAN’T SEE ANYTHING AND IT’S THE GREATEST MOMENT IN SPORTS HISTORY!"
Cass says, "Blurt I’m crying in the dark and I don’t care who hears it, put it in my contract, I’m crying!"
The lights slam back on.
APEX PRIME: all six, seated, blinking, betrayed by their own certainty. The Sump: Dutch, standing. And Vess, standing beside him, holding a slag she never had to throw.
The Ref says, "The Sump — the SUMP — wins the Coldwater Open!"
The arena detonates. Pip wakes up from his faint directly into a championship and screams for joy and a little from confusion.
Pip says, "Did we — WE WON? I was ASLEEP. I won a tournament ASLEEP. This is the best and least earned day of my life!"
Barnacle Bash says, "THE SEA PROVIDES! I KNEW THERE WAS WATER SOMEWHERE, AND IT WAS INSIDE US ALL ALONG!"
Merv says, "Yeah."
Coach Rusk says, "That’s three words from Merv in one day. Somebody write it down. The boy’s a poet now."
The Sump’s bench floods the pit. Even Old Pemms, furniture no longer, is carried in on a tide of people who have not won anything in a very long time.
Giles says, "A slag missed me! For the first time in my life, a slag MISSED me! The universe blinked, Lottie! It blinked!"
Lottie says, "That’s because you were unconscious under a pile of your own teammates, Giles. But we’ll call it grace."
Giles says, "I’ll take grace. I’ll take it in any form the pit will give it."
Coach Rusk, upright on his cot at the rail, watches his terrible, impossible team and does the second thing he has not done in nine years: he smiles, and lets someone see it.
Coach Rusk says, "Don’t look at me. It’s the painkillers. I’m in agony and I’m thrilled and I refuse to explain which is which."
Dutch says, "We did it, Coach. You got us here."
Coach Rusk says, "No. You got you here. I just yelled at the fern until it turned into a team. Now stop hugging me, I have a reputation and half of it is fern."
Forty thousand credits. Exactly the debt. The Sump is saved by the width of a single slag thrown in the dark.
MAXIM VIGO, flattened, approaches the pit to gloat about the one thing he has left: the money doesn’t matter, because he still owns the block.
Maxim Vigo says, "Enjoy your little trophy. You won the prize, but I still hold the paper on this whole district. I’ll flatten the Sump next quarter and call it synergy."
Vess says, "About that. As Dutch’s lawyer — a title I gave myself this morning and am prepared to defend — I’d point you to clause nine of the Open’s charter."

Vess says, "The tournament’s title sponsor forfeits all district claims within the arena’s ward if they lose the final. You sponsored the Open, Vigo. Your name’s on the banner. You made me put it there."
Maxim Vigo says, "I — that’s — nobody reads clause nine."
Vess says, "I read clause nine. I read all the clauses. It’s the one thing I was ever good at, and tonight it’s the one thing that mattered."
Maxim Vigo says, "You worked for ME. I optimized your salary personally. I gave you a corner office with a view of a wall I owned!"

Vess says, "You did. And every day I read the fine print for you, and every day I hated that the fine print was always on your side. Tonight it wasn’t. You have no idea how good it feels to be on the side of the small print for once."
Maxim Vigo says, "This is a betrayal."
Vess says, "This is a CONTRACT, Vigo. You worship them right up until one of them worships back at someone else. Clause nine. Signed, sponsored, and self-inflicted."
Coach Rusk says, "She’s better than any slugger I ever coached and she plays a sport made entirely of paper. Remind me to never owe her money."
Vess says, "You already do, Coach. I’m billing the Sump for the semifinal fingerprint analysis. Family rate. But I’m billing it."
Vigo looks at his own name on the banner above the pit — the banner he demanded — and understands, for the first time in his optimized life, that he pre-lost.

Dutch says, "Here’s the thing about the Sump, Vigo. You can’t flatten a place people keep coming back to. You can only join it. First round’s on the house. You look like you need to sit down somewhere that isn’t optimized."
Maxim Vigo says, "I don’t — I have never once had a beer in a building I didn’t own."
Lottie says, "Then you’re overdue, sweetheart. Sit. Mind the beam. She’s earned her rest and so, God help us, have we."

And here is the small twist the Sump never advertised. Weeks ago, when the odds against them were posted at forty to one, Dutch walked to a bookmaker and did the only reckless thing a careful man ever does.
Dutch says, "I bet on us, Vess. Everything I had left. Forty credits, at forty to one."
Vess says, "Dutch. Forty at forty to one is — that’s sixteen hundred credits, not forty thousand. That doesn’t save the bar."

Dutch says, "No. But it buys a round for everyone in this pit tonight, and it means the one person in Coldwater who believed we’d win — was me. First time in my life I put money on myself. Felt terrible. Felt incredible. Felt like the Sump."
Vess says, "You reckless, sentimental, structurally-optimistic man. Give me the betting slip. I’m going to frame it next to clause nine."
Maxim Vigo says, "You people bet on YOURSELVES? At forty to one? That’s — that’s financially insane. That’s not a strategy, that’s a feeling with a receipt."
Dutch says, "Yeah, Vigo. That’s the Sump. A feeling with a receipt. Sit down. Lottie’s bringing you a beer you didn’t optimize and can’t return."
And so the Sump kept its pit, its beam, its waitress, its pirate, its silent giant, its fainting champion, its heartbroken romantic — and gained a lawyer, a coach, and one deeply confused CEO.
Coach Rusk says, "Don’t get sentimental. You’re all still terrible. You just won ONCE. That’s not a career. That’s an accident with witnesses."
Dutch says, "Coach. Admit it. You believed in us."

Coach Rusk says, "I believed in the fern more than I believed in you, and the fern never won an Open. So maybe. Wheel me to the bar. And Dutch — good game. Don’t tell anyone I said it. I have a reputation for being in a fern."
Dutch says, "Vess. That feeling from the pit. Did we ever file it?"
Vess says, "No. I lost the paperwork on purpose. First time in my life. Let’s leave it unfiled and see what it does."
Over at the bar, Vigo nurses his first-ever unowned beer with the wary suspicion of a man who has never trusted a thing he didn’t buy.
Maxim Vigo says, "This is — the beer is warm. The stool wobbles. The beam is making a sound I would have condemned this building for."
Lottie says, "That’s the Sump, sweetheart. Nothing works and nobody leaves."
Maxim Vigo says, "It’s horrible. I — I don’t hate it. That’s the horrible part. Why don’t I hate it?"

Coach Rusk says, "Because for the first time in your life nobody in this room wants anything from you, Vigo. No tier. No fee. Turns out that’s the one thing you couldn’t optimize: being left alone with a warm beer and no leverage. Enjoy it. It’s free. It’s the only thing here that is."
Maxim Vigo says, "I could buy this feeling."
Dutch says, "You could. But you’d own it, and then it’d be work, and then it wouldn’t be this. Just drink the beer, Vigo. Mind the beam."
She takes his hand. Giles bursts into tears of joy at a love that is not his, which is, for Giles, the purest kind.
Giles says, "THIS is why you come back to the Sump. You come back for the day the pit finally throws something good at somebody."
The Sump never became famous. It never got optimized. The beam never got fixed — they named it, instead, and bought it a drink on anniversaries.

But every year, on the night of the Open, a wrecked old coach and a bar full of terrible, stubborn people crowd around a neon pit — and remember the year the last ones standing were the ones the whole city told to sit down.
That’s Slagball. You throw. You get hit. You catch what you can. And if you’re very lucky, and very stubborn, you get to come back.
name: Slagball
